posts.html:
The Eastern Ghats are among the oldest exposed mountain systems on the planet. Their geological substrate — predominantly khondalite, charnockite, and granite of Archaean to Proterozoic age — records crustal growth processes spanning 3.0 to 0.5 billion years, with tectonic domains that participated in the assembly and breakup of supercontinents Columbia and Rodinia (Bose et al. 2011; Dasgupta et al. 2013). The Eastern Ghats Belt preserves deep crustal sections that are considered analogous to deeply eroded Himalayan-type settings (Dobmeier & Raith 2003), yet unlike the Himalayas and the Western Ghats, they have received a fraction of the scientific and policy attention.

This is a discontinuous chain of hills extending approximately 1,750 km from the Mahanadi River in Odisha to the Vaigai in Tamil Nadu, covering roughly 75,000 km² across five states — Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu (Jayakumar et al. 2009; Behera et al. 2024). The average elevation is around 600 m, but the range spans sea level to 1,680 m at Arma Konda. This span encompasses tropical dry deciduous forest, tropical dry evergreen forest, scrub, thorn woodland, and patches of semi-evergreen and moist deciduous forest — a vegetational heterogeneity that reflects the complex interplay of rainfall, elevation, substrate, and palaeohistory across the Deccan (Meher-Homji 1977; Champion & Seth 1968; Ratnam et al. 2016). The Eastern Ghats harbour more than 3,200 species of flowering plants, whose diversity reflects geographical, climatic, and altitudinal variation across a phytogeographic region characterised by the co-existence of plant lineages with Himalayan, northeast Indian, and Western Ghats affinities (Kadavul & Parthasarathy 1999; Sivaraj et al. 2020; Warrier et al. 2020). Tropical dry evergreen forests, in particular, are largely restricted to the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, making them a vegetation type of global rarity.

The faunal and floral links of the Deccan Peninsula to the ancient southern supercontinent Gondwanaland are evident in the presence of relict lineages with biological affinities to Africa, Madagascar, and Sri Lanka. The peninsula's biogeographic history — its northward drift, collision with Laurasia, and subsequent climatic oscillations — has produced patterns of endemism that remain poorly resolved, particularly in the dry zones east of the Western Ghats (Karanth 2006; Vijayakumar et al. 2016; Bossuyt et al. 2004). New species continue to be described from the Eastern Ghats across taxa: recent herpetofaunal inventories of the Central Eastern Ghats recorded 105 species of amphibians and reptiles, including new range extensions and rare species, from a single 300-day survey effort (Ganesh et al. 2021). Five new microendemic Cnemaspis species were described from the Shevaroy massif alone (Agarwal et al. 2022). Many taxa remain known only from their type localities. Significant squamate diversity — gekkonids, scincids, colubrids — includes several taxa endemic or largely restricted to the scrub forests of peninsular India, and mesic forests in these ranges remain poorly explored, likely concealing undescribed species (Ganesh & Chandramouli 2018).

And yet, the Eastern Ghats have no equivalent of the Western Ghats' biodiversity hotspot designation. They receive no comparable institutional investment, no dedicated research infrastructure, and no sustained funding pipeline. The consequences are predictable. Mining, industrialisation, and habitat clearance proceed without the friction of recognition. Bauxite, manganese, and iron ore extraction are among the fastest-growing threats (Forest Survey of India; Zoological Survey of India). Long-term land use studies show that between 1920 and 2015, the Eastern Ghats experienced extensive forest loss to agricultural expansion, infrastructure development, and mining, with consequences for landscape connectivity (Ramachandran et al. 2018). Invasive species — Lantana camara, Prosopis juliflora — outcompete native flora across degraded tracts. The protected area network is thin and unevenly distributed; its effectiveness is routinely questioned (Reddy & Satheesh 1997). The discontinuous nature of the hill ranges, separated by major river valleys and anthropogenic landscapes, provides a unique natural system for investigating species distributions, endemism, population genetics, and evolutionary diversification — but only if someone actually does the work (Bossuyt et al. 2004).

The disparity is not one of ecological value. It is one of knowledge. The Western Ghats have been studied intensively for over a century; the Eastern Ghats have not. Soil chemistry, geomorphology, phytochemistry, population dynamics of plant species, and the spatial ecology of most vertebrate and invertebrate taxa remain unaddressed in any systematic way (Sudhakar Reddy et al. 2008; Dutta & Mohapatra 2017; Dash & Mohapatra 2025). There is no comprehensive molecular barcode library for Eastern Ghats flora. The trophic ecology of even medically important snake species across peninsular India has never been studied using modern methods. Conservation in the Eastern Ghats, to the extent it exists, operates largely without an understanding of the organisms it aims to protect — their evolutionary histories, ecological specialisations, physiological limits, or population structure.

About CEGS Foundation

The Centre for Eastern Ghats Studies is a research institution dedicated exclusively to advancing the conservation biology, ecology, and evolutionary biology of the Eastern Ghats and the adjoining peninsular plains. Recognising that the region remains one of India's least-studied biodiversity landscapes, CEGS seeks to build the scientific foundation necessary for effective, evidence-based conservation.

Our work integrates field ecology, taxonomy, evolutionary biology, molecular biology, spatial analysis, and long-term ecological monitoring to understand the processes that shape biodiversity. By generating high-quality scientific knowledge, CEGS supports habitat restoration, species conservation, ecological planning, and informed environmental policy.

As a field research station, laboratory, and collaborative scientific platform, CEGS undertakes original research, supports postgraduate and doctoral training, contributes to IUCN Red List assessments, documents biodiversity through species descriptions and inventories, and publishes in peer-reviewed scientific journals. The institution is committed to producing rigorous science that directly informs conservation action across the Eastern Ghats bioregion.

Mission

To generate rigorous scientific knowledge on the biodiversity, ecology, and evolutionary history of the Eastern Ghats through interdisciplinary research, long-term ecological monitoring, and field-based conservation science.

CEGS aims to strengthen conservation by:

  • Conducting high-quality research in conservation biology, ecology, taxonomy, evolutionary biology, and landscape ecology.
  • Building long-term biodiversity datasets to understand ecological change and guide conservation decisions.
  • Supporting habitat restoration through scientific research on ecosystem processes and native biodiversity.
  • Contributing to species assessments, conservation planning, and environmental policy using robust scientific evidence.
  • Training the next generation of conservation scientists through field research, laboratory studies, and academic collaborations.
  • Establishing the Eastern Ghats as one of India's best-documented and scientifically understood biodiversity regions.

Vision

To become the leading centre for research on the Eastern Ghats, internationally recognised for advancing knowledge in ecology, evolutionary biology, and conservation science.

CEGS envisions a future where conservation decisions are grounded in rigorous scientific evidence, native ecosystems are restored and resilient, and the extraordinary biodiversity of the Eastern Ghats is understood, protected, and valued for generations to come. Through excellence in research, collaboration, and scientific training, the institution seeks to establish the Eastern Ghats as a globally important landscape for biodiversity research and conservation.

By committing to sustained, long-term ecological monitoring, we generate the high-quality scientific evidence required to bridge the gap between foundational knowledge and evidence-based conservation action in the Eastern Ghats.

posts.html:
Native Forest Nursery

The Eastern Ghats Native Forest Nursery serves as the foundation of our ecological restoration efforts by propagating indigenous tree, shrub, climber, and grass species native to the dry deciduous forests of Peninsular India. Rather than maximizing the number of saplings produced, the nursery focuses on preserving local genetic diversity by collecting seeds from naturally occurring populations across different landscapes. Each species is propagated based on its ecological role, ensuring that restoration supports the recovery of entire forest communities rather than individual tree species. The nursery also functions as a living repository for native flora, supporting research, education, habitat restoration, and long-term conservation planning.

The unique niches of the Dry Deciduous Forests of Krishnagiri, where our campus lies

The dry deciduous forests of the Eastern Ghats are dynamic ecosystems shaped by seasonal rainfall, prolonged dry periods, rocky terrain, and varied elevations. Within these forests, every habitat—from rocky outcrops and hill slopes to seasonal streams, grasslands, bamboo thickets, and forest edges—provides specialized ecological niches for different plants, insects, reptiles, birds, and mammals. These diverse microhabitats support complex interactions between species, allowing biodiversity to thrive even in landscapes that may appear sparse during the dry season. Conserving this habitat diversity is essential for maintaining the ecological resilience of the Eastern Ghats.

Other services

Biodiversity Assessments

If you own or manage land located close to a reserve forest, protected area, or other important natural habitats, CEGS can help document and understand the biodiversity of your property. Our team can undertake field-based biodiversity assessments covering vegetation, birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians, insects, and other relevant taxa, depending on the landscape and objectives. These assessments can establish a baseline of species and habitats, identify areas of ecological significance, and provide information to guide responsible land management, restoration, and conservation planning.

Note : Assessment costs are determined on a project-by-project basis, depending on the location, size and accessibility of the property, duration of fieldwork, taxa being assessed, team requirements, travel, accommodation, and other logistical requirements. Contact us on info@cegs.org to discuss your site and assessment objectives.

Aishwarya is a wildlife biologist, specialised in herpetology. Her enthusiasm for field-based biodiversity surveys shaped her research path. Along with her passion for behaviour-based studies and evolutionary biology, her main focus lies on trophic ecology.

She has travelled across different landscapes of the Southern Peninsular India and the Andaman and Nicobar archipelagos as a student, field assistant, biodiversity council member and research fellow, with a keen interest in working in wildlife and conservation. Her current academic interest focuses on the Eastern Ghats and its understudied and undervalued biodiversity, particularly snakes. She works with a special interest towards documentation and conservation of the lesser-known taxa of these fragmented hillocks.

In the process of grasping the conservational facets of the landscape and its wildlife, she aids in elucidating the complexities of human-wildlife relationships and community-orientated conservational strategies.

Her childhood curiosity about the exotic ecosystems inhabited by dinosaurs and creatures from the African savanna has facilitated in establishing her strategic vision with scientific requirements for conservation of our local biodiversity.

One could say, “She is your friendly neighbourhood ecologist."

posts.html:
Arjun Viswa specializes in herpetology, landscape ecology, evolutionary ecology, and conservation biology. His research combines field-based biodiversity surveys, taxonomic research, trophic ecology, and spatial distribution modeling, integrating laboratory-based molecular work with historical museum specimens to document and understand lesser-known and threatened taxa. He has worked as a research fellow on conservation and biodiversity projects across diverse landscapes of India, from the Ghats to the oceanic islands.

His research also involves human–wildlife interactions and animal behavior, focusing on the social and landscape attributes to help reduce human–wildlife conflict and develop effective conservation strategies. Since 2023, he has focused on documenting and protecting the biodiversity of the Eastern Ghats, particularly threatened and lesser-known taxa, and has contributed to IUCN Red List assessments, especially for species endemic to the region. His long-term goal is to strengthen scientific understanding and conservation of the Eastern Ghats as a globally significant biodiversity hotspot.

posts.html:
Navadharani is an arachnologist and wildlife researcher with a master’s degree in wildlife biology. She is fascinated by arachnids and primarily focuses on understudied groups, including Amblypygi (whip spiders), Uropygi (whip scorpions), and Mygalomorphs (tarantulas), among the most neglected arachnid groups in India.

As a researcher, her current work focuses on the Integrative Systematic revision of Indian Amblypygi, Uropygi, and Mygalomorphs using molecular approaches. This research aims to elucidate their species diversity, distribution patterns, evolutionary ecology, ecological significance and conservation biology. Despite their abundance and vital ecological roles, arachnids are often dismissed as backyard creatures rather than recognized as an important part of wildlife.  Her ultimate goal is to change perceptions of Arachnids and promote greater recognition of their ecological importance and the need for their conservation.

posts.html:
Dr. Kanivalan Iwar a botanist, his research interests broadly include plant taxonomy and systematics, biological diversity, plant community ecology, agrobiodiversity, and plant genetic resources. He did long-term research in the Southern Western Ghats mountains and documented species diversity, distributions, vegetation structure, and ecologically important taxa. Through this, he acquired a broad spectrum of expertise, including taxa inventorying, identification, herbarium work, eco-community analysis, and floristic assessment. He has a special interest in rare, endemic, and threatened taxa.

Well along, he worked on the characterization and conservation of plant genetic resources at the National Agrobiodiversity Center–Genebank, National Institute of Agricultural Sciences, Rural Development Administration, Republic of Korea, where he expanded his international research experience, which covered seed micromorphology and morphological and phenotypic analyses of Allium germplasm. Through this experience, he integrated cutting-edge laboratory and analytical methods with conventional plant science.

With an emphasis on understanding the richness, distribution, taxonomy, evolutionary relationships, and conservation status of woody plant species, his current research is on Dendrophy of the Eastern Ghats. To provide a thorough knowledge of the woody flora of the Eastern Ghats, the project incorporates molecular systematics, ecology, phylogeographic techniques, and climate-change perspectives. In this, complex taxa, endemism and vulnerable groups, as well as their genetic and ecological linkages and their susceptibility to environmental and climatic changes, have received special attention. His goal is to contribute to the long-term conservation, evolutionary understanding, taxonomic resolution, and documentation of the Eastern Ghats' woody plant diversity through this effort. To provide trustworthy scientific information for biodiversity conservation and the sustainable management of plant genetic resources, his broader research objective is to integrate conventional plant taxonomy with molecular, ecological, spatial, and computational methodologies.
